newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Strike leaders rebuff S.Korean ruling party head.
newsitem.headline: Strike leaders rebuff S.Korean ruling party head.

text.p: The chairman of South Korea's ruling party made a dramatic visit on Monday to a Seoul cathedral where union leaders are sheltering from arrest as they plot the biggest strike in the nation's history.
But Lee Hong-koo was turned away by heads of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions.
Instead, he met the Roman Catholic cardinal of South Korea and was lectured by him on worker welfare.

"Get out, get out", workers chanted as the New Korea Party chairman pulled up in his limousine outside Myongdong Cathedral, where seven union leaders are directing wildcat industrial action from a ramshackle tent.
A union official said strike leaders would only meet Lee if the government revoked a labour law that has sparked industrial unrest and withdrew arrest warrants against them.

The confederation has threatened to bring out all its 500,000 members on Wednesday, joining an all-out stoppage by the 1.2 million-strong Federation of Korean Trade Unions scheduled to begin on Tuesday.
It is the first time the two union umbrella bodies have coordinated full-blown industrial action.
The law allows employers to lay off workers -- almost unheard of in South Korea -- and replace strikers. It also delays official recognition of the confederation until 2000.
Lee skirted close to the strike tent on his way to a cathedral building for a meeting with Cardinal Kim Soo-hwan.
"I'm sorry and embarrassed for causing you trouble," Lee told the spirtual head of the country's 3.5 million Roman Catholics.

The cardinal replied: "I understand you have passed a law to save the economy, but I hope we all understand that to love this country we have to increase the quality of life for workers as well as save the economy".
On Saturday Lee challenged union leaders to a televised debate over the law, but confederation leader Kwon Young-kil dismissed the offer as a propaganda ploy.
Buoyant strike leaders, claiming public opinion was on their side, are plotting to idle key parts of South Korea's usually roaring export machine and cause massive disruption to public services.
The military is standing up to keep essential services running.
Media reports said a force of 2,500 military specialists had been trained to take over from railway drivers and telecommunications workers.
"If anything happens, the military will be mobilised," a defence ministry spokesman said.

Federation leaders have urged power, port and railway workers to go on partial strike and all others to join a total shutdown on Tuesday. Buses, subways, hospitals, banks, hotels, taxis, newspapers and state industries will be hit.
The confederation controls union workers at state telecommunications giant Korea Telecom and at the giant Hyundai and Daewoo groups.
Tension was running high in the southeast city of Ulsan where unionists are occupying the offices of Hyundai Motor Co, the country's biggest auto plant, in what they call a "return to work struggle".
Last week, management shut down the car plant that had been crippled by a go-slow by union workers. Unions claimed it was a lockout and broke into the factory in defiance.
Official figures showed production losses from strikes so far would cost the country 1.96 trillion won ($2.3 billion) by the end of Monday.
The previous biggest industrial action was in 1989 when some 400,000 workers downed tools by official count. However, those strikes dragged on for months.
